pages.title: Xin chào
pages.summary: Hello (universal greeting)

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: For travelers, Xin chào is the most dependable hello. It is polite, short, and safe when you walk into a shop, step up to a hotel desk, meet a guide, or start a simple request. In everyday Vietnamese, greetings often depend on age, gender, and relationship, so the next step is learning when to use chào plus a relationship word. If you are unsure, Xin chào lets you begin warmly without guessing the other person's role.

sections.title: Quick say
sections.body: Use Xin chào when you want one safe greeting. Use Chào when the moment is relaxed and the person already feels familiar.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: Xin gives the greeting a polite shape, chào carries the hello, and the full phrase is the safest default when you do not know the relationship word yet.

sections.title: Situational greetings
sections.body: Use these when the setting is more specific: a friend, a respectful adult, a phone call, or a time-of-day greeting.

sections.title: How locals actually greet
sections.body: This is the most local pattern. Pick the relationship word when the person's role is clear; stay with Xin chào when you are unsure. These words are not just family labels. In Vietnam they also show respect, age relationship, and social distance, which is why a greeting can sound warmer when the relationship word fits.

phrases.english: Hello, older brother / slightly older man
Hello, older sister / slightly older woman

sections.title: Common follow-ups
sections.body: After hello, small talk often checks health, movement, or the social moment. Use these when the exchange has room to continue.

sections.title: Cultural note
sections.body: Vietnamese greetings carry relationship information. Learning the pattern matters more than memorizing one perfect hello. You do not need to guess perfectly as a visitor; a calm Xin chào is accepted almost everywhere. As you get more comfortable, adding anh, chị, em, cô, chú, ông, or bà makes the greeting feel less like a phrasebook line and more like a real local opening.

sections.body: Cảm ơn answers the traveler question "Thank you" in small service and first-contact moments. Say this anytime someone helps you, serves you, or gives directions. A short thank-you keeps service moments warm and simple. Its job is giving the other person a simple anchor rather than a long explanation. The forms below show how tone, setting, or politeness changes the best choice.

This is for when someone is speaking too quickly or using unfamiliar words. Lead with this before you ask for a repeat or a simpler version. Its job is asking for one clear help action before adding more words. Expect a slower repeat, a pointed explanation, or a switch to writing; then use Explore next if the reply creates another small task.

pages.title: Dạ
pages.summary: Use Dạ as a polite yes, a respectful opener, or a soft way to show you are listening.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Dạ is one of the most useful small words in Vietnamese. It can answer yes, show that you heard someone, soften the start of a sentence, or make a short reply sound respectful. Travelers should learn it as a polite response marker first, then choose Có, Không, Được, or Đúng when the answer itself needs to be clear.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Use Dạ when someone older, staff, a driver, or a local helper speaks to you and you want to answer politely before the main information.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The whole word is short, so the useful lesson is what it does in the conversation.

breakdown.english: respectful yes / I hear you / softens the answer

sections.title: Answer choices
sections.body: Dạ can come before an answer, but these words carry the answer itself.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it when a staff member asks a question, when an older person speaks first, when you are confirming that you heard instructions, or when you want to sound gentle before a short request. It works beautifully before Chào anh, Cảm ơn, or a yes/no answer.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Dạ does not replace every yes. If the person needs a clear answer, say Dạ first if you want, then add Có, Không, Được, or Đúng.

sections.title: Explore next
sections.body: These are natural next steps after a polite acknowledgment.

pages.title: Đúng
pages.summary: Use Đúng when you want to confirm that something is correct.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Đúng means yes in the sense of correct or right. Use it when someone checks a name, room number, pickup place, price, order, or direction and you want to confirm they have it right. It is different from Có, which often answers whether something exists or is available.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Say Đúng when the other person is checking a fact and you want a short confirmation.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The word points to correctness, not just agreement.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it when staff point to your booking name, a driver repeats the destination, a cashier confirms the item, or someone asks whether a detail is correct.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: For extra politeness, Dạ đúng is natural in many adult service moments, but Đúng by itself is still clear when the exchange is quick.

pages.title: Được

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Được is the compact okay when a plan works, a suggested option is acceptable, or someone asks whether something is possible. It is not just yes; it often means can, okay, allowed, or that works in context.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Use Được when you want to accept a practical option without adding a long sentence.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: Think of it as permission, possibility, and acceptance packed into one short word.

It works with peers, friendly helpers, classmates, younger adults near your age, or someone whose role feels casual rather than formal. If the person is clearly older or in a service role, Chào anh or Chào chị may sound warmer.

sections.title: Good to know
